'''''Sedum acre''''', commonly known as the '''goldmoss stonecrop''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SEAC|taxon=Sedum acre|accessdate=9 November 2015}}</ref> '''mossy stonecrop''',<ref>Dickinson, T.; Metsger, D.; Bull, J.; & Dickinson, R. (2004) ROM Field Guide to Wildflowers of Ontario. Toronto:Royal Ontario Museum, p. 243.</ref> '''goldmoss sedum''', '''biting stonecrop''',<ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=44}}</ref> and '''wallpepper''', is a perennial [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Crassulaceae]]. It is native to Europe, northern and western Asia and North Africa, but is also naturalised in North America,<ref name="Moroore">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YYI4AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA146 |page=146 |title=Flora of the British Isles |first1=A. R. |last1=Clapham |first2=T. G. |last2=Tutin |first3=David Moresby |last3= Moore |publisher=CUP Archive |year=1987}}</ref> southern South America,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sedum acre L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:274996-1 |access-date=2025-02-16 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> Japan,{{cn|date=July 2024}} and New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sedum acre |author= |work=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |date= |access-date=24 July 2024 |url= https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/sedum-acre/}}</ref>

==Description==
The biting stonecrop is a tufted [[evergreen]] perennial that forms mat-like stands some {{convert|5|to|12|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall. For much of the year, the stems are short, semi-prostrate and densely clad in leaves. At the flowering time in June and July, the stems lengthen and are erect, somewhat limp and often pinkish-brown with the leaves further apart. The leaves are alternate, fleshy and shortly cylindrical with a rounded tip. They are also sometimes tinged with red. The starry flowers form a three to six-flowered [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]]. The calyx has five fleshy sepals fused at the base, the corolla consists of five regular bright yellow petals, there are ten stamens, a separate gynoecium and five pistils. The fruit consists of five united, many-seeded [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]]. The leaves contain an acrid fluid that can cause skin rashes.<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/biting-stonecrop |title=Biting stonecrop: ''Sedum acre'' |publisher=NatureGate |access-date=29 December 2013}}</ref>

==Habitat==
Biting stonecrop is a low-growing plant that cannot compete with more vigorous, fast-growing species. It is specially adapted for growing on thin dry soils and can be found on dry grassland, shingle, beaches, drystone walls, dry banks, seashore rocks, roadside verges, wasteland and in sandy meadows near the sea.<ref name="Moroore"/><ref name=NatureGate/>

==Cultivation==
Biting stonecrop spreads when allowed to do so, but is easily controlled, being shallow-rooted. It is used in [[hanging basket]]s and [[container garden]]s, as a trailing accent, in [[Herbaceous border|borders]], or as groundcover.  This plant grows as a creeping [[ground cover]], often in dry sandy [[soil]], but also in the cracks of [[masonry]]. It grows well in poor soils, sand, rock gardens, and rich garden soil, under a variety of light levels.

Biting stonecrop is said to have a peppery taste (hence the name "biting") and is sometimes used in herbal medicine. However, it is considered to be poisonous and consumption is discouraged.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.agfonds.lv/herbs/herbs-a-b/biting-stonecrop-sedum-acre/ |title=Biting stonecrop Sedum acre |access-date=2 August 2024}}</ref>
